minutes.headline: Task force fine-tuned its draft public presentation on a proposed town-wide stormwater utility fee; no fee was set.
minutes.summary: The Stormwater Task Force spent the meeting line-by-line reviewing a draft slide presentation and a separate FAQ document to be shown at an upcoming public meeting on a proposed stormwater utility fee. Members discussed sample fee tables for residential and commercial properties, comparisons to peer towns, the case for a dedicated stormwater program manager, and the approval process, but took no vote other than to adjourn.

budget_items.topic: Average single-family home value used in fee illustration
budget_items.what_was_said: The average home value in Lunenburg was cited to anchor the middle tier of an illustrative residential fee table.

budget_items.topic: Storm water budget figure used in fee-impact example
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the example used an older, smaller total storm water budget figure rather than the newer, larger one, which changes the resulting fee percentages.

budget_items.topic: Property-tax-based method for illustrating fee equivalents (residential A/B/C)
budget_items.what_was_said: A member proposed showing what residents already pay toward stormwater through property taxes, using the town's tax rate and the storm water budget's share of the total tax levy.

budget_items.topic: Old vs. new storm water budget total used in percentage calculations
budget_items.what_was_said: Members compared results from dividing the old, smaller budget figure versus the new, larger figure by the town's total tax levy.
A calculation for a small residential property showed it would pay more under the flat utility fee than it currently contributes through taxes, raising concern about that message.

budget_items.topic: Upper-tier cap for large commercial properties
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant's original proposal had capped large commercial parcel fees at one level; the task force previously rejected that cap and discussed extrapolating tiers upward instead, to preserve revenue and room for partial abatements.
A tax-exempt church property, currently paying nothing, would owe a new fee under the proposed structure, illustrating a new revenue source the utility would capture.

budget_items.topic: Large commercial fee example from a peer town (Dennis)
budget_items.what_was_said: A shopping complex in Dennis, MA was cited as paying a very high storm water fee under that town's tiered structure, used as a comparison point.

budget_items.topic: Estimated total impervious area and revenue-share correlation
budget_items.what_was_said: Members recalculated the number of parcels times average impervious area, producing updated percentages for the table showing how revenue share compares to impervious-area share.

budget_items.topic: Cap on stormwater credit/abatement for good housekeeping practices
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force discussed capping credits/abatements at a percentage of the fee, based on what other Massachusetts communities with utilities offer.

budget_items.topic: Assumed revenue loss from abatement program
budget_items.what_was_said: A rule of thumb from other communities assumes a portion of revenue will be lost to abatements once the credit program is in place, and some towns budget higher in year one to compensate.

budget_items.topic: Estimated replacement value of town storm water infrastructure
budget_items.what_was_said: A wide range was initially used to estimate the value of the town's storm drainage network; the task force agreed to use the higher end on the slide.

budget_items.topic: Estimated miles of storm drain pipe and roads with storm infrastructure
budget_items.what_was_said: Rough estimates of pipe and road mileage were used to size the infrastructure-value slide; a member said these need to be verified with the DPW's own figures.

budget_items.topic: Infrastructure valuation framed as a park comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: The estimated value of the storm water network was compared to a large capital asset to make the scale tangible to residents.

budget_items.topic: Number of properties and parcels in the fee dataset
budget_items.what_was_said: The rate-structure analysis covers a defined subset of properties out of the town's full assessor's parcel list, with impervious area to be entered for each.

budget_items.topic: DPW operating budget request for storm water items ahead of the utility
budget_items.what_was_said: Bill said an extra amount was added to the DPW operational budget this cycle in case the utility fee is not approved in time, though he expects it may not survive budget cuts.

Using the state's override calculator, the group modeled what an increase to the general tax levy (covering basin cleaning, sweeping, and added engineering needs) would cost an average homeowner, as an alternative to the flat utility fee.

decisions.decision: Bill agreed to bring hard copies of the FAQ document to hand out at the public meeting.
Keep the residential/commercial fee-impact comparison slide (with the added revenue column), to be refined once real numbers are added.
Add a caveat to the presentation noting the fee is not guaranteed to stay flat, given uncertainty from a pending new EPA stormwater permit.
Keep the 50% cap on credits/abatements in the presentation, consistent with other Massachusetts communities.
Leave fee-structure governance with the select board for now rather than pursuing a combined sewer/storm commission, since that would require a multi-year legislative process.
Remove the 'drainage improvement projects' line item from the funding-use slide since it is not currently budgeted through the utility.
Bill's GIS team will go back and delineate impervious area for previously miscoded properties (e.g., Jaclyn Drive) that lacked a proper land-use code.
John will independently build his own spreadsheet model from the impervious-area data to test rate-structure trade-offs, in parallel with the consultant's team.
Someone will contact the library the next day to confirm the room and whether a screen/projector will be available for the presentation.
Hold audience questions until after the full slideshow is presented, given the likely larger turnout for this meeting.
The FAQ document will not be further revised for now; Jarice will send a final revised slide deck by end of day the next day.
Meeting adjourned at 8:26 p.m. on March 3, 2026.

what_happened.line: The task force decided the fee structure stays under select board oversight rather than pursuing a separate sewer/storm commission, which would need a multi-year legislative process.
Members kept a 50% cap on stormwater credits and abatements in the public presentation, matching what other Massachusetts communities with similar utilities offer.
A caveat will be added noting the proposed fee is not guaranteed to stay flat, given uncertainty from a pending new EPA stormwater permit.
A funding-use slide line item for drainage improvement projects was removed because that work is not currently budgeted through the utility.
No fee amount was set; the meeting was spent revising slides and an FAQ ahead of an upcoming public presentation, with a final deck due from Jarice the next day.

why_it_matters: This is preparation for a proposed town-wide stormwater fee that would appear on future water/sewer or tax bills; no rate has been adopted yet.
Keeping fee governance with the select board, rather than creating a new sewer/storm commission, means the same elected board residents already interact with would continue to set this fee.
A 50% cap on credits limits how much a property owner could reduce the fee through stormwater management practices, and the fee amount itself is described as unstable pending a new EPA permit.
